title: Region drain hysteresis bug and tier fallback cascade — incident postmortem and remediation
creator: Amaya Chen
description: During a routine traffic shift for capacity rebalancing in eu-west, several backend hosts were marked draining prematurely due to a mis-aggregated latency signal. That drain triggered tier-based rerouting which pushed traffic to a lower-tier quantized variant and then to alternate regions. The resulting sudden capacity pressure on those variants caused further stalls and fallback oscillation across region/tier boundaries, increasing end-to-end latency and 5xx rates for ~28 minutes for EU customers. This ticket captures the incident timeline, root cause analysis, immediate mitigations, and discrete follow-ups to prevent recurrence.
incident_summary: At 2026-03-04T09:12:00Z the routing controller started initiating drains for a subset of eu-west hosts after a burst of short-lived latency spikes was interpreted as sustained degradation. Drains applied without adequate hysteresis and with a bug in the aggregation window caused >30% of eu-west capacity to drain within 90s. Smart routing subsequently applied tier-preference rules that routed traffic to quantized model variants in eu-central and to hosted fallback in us-east. Those variants lacked the reserved pool capacity and warmed caches, resulting in KV cache misses and backend stalls that fed further latency signals. Automatic fallback policies then flipped routes back and forth between region/tier variants for ~28 minutes before on-call applied a manual override at 09:40Z to pin routes to stable variants. Impact: elevated token latency (p95 increased from 180ms to 1.2s) and a spike in 5xx from 0.12% to 3.8% for affected routes.
timeline:
2026-03-04 09:09 UTC — Planned micro-deployment started: autoscaler policy change in eu-west (no change to routing config expected)
2026-03-04 09:12 UTC — First latency spike observed on several eu-west pods (bursts from external load test and external partner traffic). Aggregator computed rolling 90s p95 incorrectly (off-by-factor in scale), flagged pods unhealthy.
2026-03-04 09:13 UTC — Routing controller started drain cycle: 12/35 eu-west serving pods entered DRAIN state within 90s.
2026-03-04 09:14 UTC — Smart routing tier rules redirected new sessions to quantized variants in eu-central and hosted fallback in us-east.
2026-03-04 09:15–09:30 UTC — Quantized variants experienced cold KV caches and high CPU; additional latency propagated into health signals leading to further drains and cross-region rerouting. Oscillation began.
2026-03-04 09:28 UTC — Alert: Routing error budget burn >75% for eu routes; on-call paged.
2026-03-04 09:32 UTC — Engineering triage: began temporarily raising drain hysteresis and pinning a subset of flows to stable variants.
2026-03-04 09:40 UTC — Manual routing override applied to stop oscillation; traffic stabilized over 6 minutes.
2026-03-04 10:05 UTC — Post-incident verification completed; metrics returned to baseline by 10:20 UTC.
root_cause: Two coupled issues: 1) Aggregation bug in the rolling-latency calculator caused transient spikes to be treated as sustained degradation when the scale factor applied to p95 was incorrect for short windows. The bug manifests only under bursty traffic and a changed autoscaler pattern. 2) Routing controller had insufficient hysteresis/debounce for drain transitions and lacked a cross-region backoff when tier fallback events were occurring. Together these allowed a positive feedback loop: drains -> tier/routing fallback -> cold caches -> latency -> more drains.
immediate_mitigation: 1) Applied manual routing override to pin critical routes to stable model variants and disabled automatic drain for the eu-west pool for 30 minutes. 2) Increased drain hysteresis and extended aggregation window on the latency aggregator as a stop-gap. 3) Rolled back the autoscaler micro-deploy that triggered the pattern. These actions stopped oscillation within ~6 minutes of the manual override.
long_term_actions: Fix aggregation scale bug in latency calculator and add unit/bench tests for bursty load (PR #7832)
Introduce explicit drain hysteresis and state debounce in routing controller with configurable policy per region (runtime-2.14 patch)
Add cross-region backoff when tier fallbacks are executing to prevent simultaneous capacity pressure on alternate regions
Create a routing-simulation harness to exercise drain + fallback scenarios during canary runs
Improve dashboards: token-level p95 heatmap across region/tier and a ‘drain wave’ timeline visualization
Run chaos tests that simulate cold-cache fallback to validate cache warming policies and reserved pool sizing
postmortem_notes: We underestimated the coupling between short-term autoscaler churn and routing drain sensitivity. The aggregation bug is low-probability but high-impact under bursty traffic; it was not covered by existing tests because our synthetic load generator emits steady-state traffic rather than realistic burst patterns. During the incident, the automatic fallback logic behaved as designed but without cross-layer safeguards; design intent assumed that quantized variants had sufficient cold-start capacity — that assumption is invalid for production burst scenarios. Communication: Ops and Support were notified within 3 minutes of alert; status page updates started at 09:30Z. The incident was visible to customers via increased latency and error pages; we opened a customer-facing incident report and follow-up commit to contacts for affected accounts.
follow_up_tasks: ENG-12902 - patch latency aggregator + add bursty-load unit tests (owner: Data Plane)
ENG-12903 - debounce/drain hysteresis config + runtime rollout (owner: Routing)
ENG-12904 - add routing simulation harness and canary test (owner: Reliability)
review_feedback: PM (Riya Patel): +1 on immediate mitigations; request we add customer outreach summary and revise on-call runbooks. Design (Victor Ramos): Suggest default drain hysteresis be conservative for regions with <50 pods. Security (Maya Singh): No sensitive data exposure; confirm artifacts in drive have appropriate access controls. Engineering leads approved the fixes and required a staged rollout with runtime-2.14 canary before global release.
